raw.assessment: Full assembly plausibly checks physical fit before shipping, and repeated three-compartment orders approach the time target (D2-O6). Nevertheless, combined timing cannot locate the delay (D2-O2), customer reports do not establish every packing error (D2-O3), and three unpackers needed short-partition guidance (D2-O4). Mixed batches contain the longest orders, but layout complexity confounds a switching explanation. The concrete limiting observation is overlapping widths among first-attempt and retried partitions (D2-O5): width alone does not explain insertion difficulty. These stipulated observations support hypotheses, not demonstrated remedies or pilot success.

openings.claim: Does switching between layouts increase selection/checking time independently of compartment count?
openings.delta: Separates a workflow explanation for mixed-batch delays from the inherent work of larger layouts.
openings.prediction: A switching effect would increase selection/checking time for the same layout after a different layout; inherent complexity would instead track compartment count across both sequences.
openings.probe: Use reusable sample parts for both workers to complete matched repeated-layout and alternating-layout sequences, counterbalancing sequence order and matching exterior color. Record selection, insertion, checking and packing separately, and independently audit contents. Include all three compartment counts. Limit this exploratory trial to existing resources and time compatible with the fixed delivery date.
assumptions: Reusable samples permit matched trials within spare-board and time limits.
Practice and worker differences can be recorded; small trials cannot establish pilot success.

openings.claim: An order-specific diagram identifying each short partition's destination may improve unaided arrangement when the supplied parts are correct.
openings.delta: Tests whether ambiguity in the three-layout diagram contributes to difficulty, separately from missing or incorrect components.
openings.prediction: With independently verified identical kits, customers receiving the order-specific diagram should make fewer short-partition placement errors and requests for help than customers receiving the current diagram.
openings.probe: Randomly assign the ten willing participants to the current or order-specific diagram, balancing layouts as practicable. Observe ordered-layout completion and short-partition errors without coaching. Check incremental printing cost and preparation time before adoption; preserve supplied components, reversible joints, colors, counts and delivery date.
assumptions: Diagram production fits the 500 initial and 0.40 recurring cost ceilings.
Correct-kit difficulty is partly informational rather than entirely physical.
Ten participants provide exploratory discrimination, not validation of the 90% customer target.

raw.assessment: Selection, insertion and customer placement are candidate bottlenecks; combined timing and overlapping widths do not identify their causes. Two artifact-mediated alternatives merit bounded screening, with no demonstrated success yet.

openings.claim: Hypothesis: reusable order-specific checking mats can perform part of the completeness check through one silhouette per required component and an exterior-color reference. Empty or mismatched positions expose selection errors before assembly.
openings.delta: Transfers component accounting from workers remembering a mixed order to a visible spatial inventory; retains workshop assembly.
openings.prediction: Compared with the order slip alone, mats reduce undetected missing/wrong components and checking time, especially when alternating layouts. If errors occur after checking, mats will not improve packed completeness.
openings.probe: Use at most three spare-board samples for reusable mats. Alternate matched orders between mat and current checking, timing selection, checking, insertion and packing separately; independently inspect packed contents. Stop if mat handling erases savings or cannot fit the budget and fixed delivery schedule.
assumptions: Existing templates identify every required component.
Setup fits 500 units and recurring additions stay within 0.40 per order.

openings.claim: Hypothesis: an order-matched flat kit with corresponding marks on partition ends and base slots can let customers perform initial insertion. The interface supplies placement information currently supplied by workshop assembly and the generic diagram.
openings.delta: Removes workshop insertion from fulfillment while replacing layout interpretation with direct matching; supplied parts remain dismantlable and rearrangeable.
openings.prediction: Workshop time falls only if insertion savings exceed kitting and marking costs; customer short-partition placement improves only if ambiguity, rather than insertion difficulty, dominates.
openings.probe: Use up to twelve remaining samples to screen marked kits with ten participants across ordered layouts, including short partitions. Record unaided arrangement, insertion retries, separate workshop times and material costs. Require unchanged capacity, footprint, selected counts/color and rearrangeability; screen within the fixed deadline before any adoption. Pilot targets remain at least 59/60 complete, median workshop time at most eight minutes and at least 54/60 unaided arrangements.
assumptions: Marks remain intelligible during later rearrangement.
Marking and flat-kit protection fit both cost limits.

openings.discriminator: Same-layout switching penalty versus compartment-count complexity.
openings.probe: Both workers: counterbalance repeated/alternating sequences across counts, match color; time four stages separately; audit contents.
openings.uncertainty: Practice, worker differences and sample feasibility; exploratory only.

openings.claim: Order-specific diagrams may clarify short-partition destinations.
openings.discriminator: Fewer placement errors/help requests with identical verified kits.
openings.probe: Randomize ten participants between diagrams; balance layouts; observe unaided completion; cost printing/preparation.
openings.uncertainty: Informational versus physical difficulty; ten cannot validate 90%.

openings.claim: Reusable silhouette/color mats may externalize completeness checking while retaining workshop assembly.
openings.discriminator: Fewer missed errors and shorter checks, especially alternating layouts; downstream errors persist.
openings.probe: Use at most three board samples; alternate matched mat/current checks; time four stages; inspect packed contents.
openings.uncertainty: Template completeness, variant distinguishability, handling overhead and cost.

openings.claim: Marked order-matched flat kits may transfer initial insertion to customers.
openings.discriminator: Insertion savings exceed kitting/marking; placement improves only if ambiguity dominates physical difficulty.
openings.probe: Up to twelve remaining samples, ten participants across layouts: record unaided completion, retries, workshop stages and costs.
openings.uncertainty: Customer acceptance, later rearrangement legibility and protective packaging cost.

post_distill.decision: Screen within existing resources/deadline; no proven remedy. All require 30x20 cm footprint, same capacity, reversible joints, selected counts/color, initial cost <=500 and recurring addition <=0.40. Reject adoption violating these or erasing time savings. Pilot targets: >=59/60 complete, median <=8 minutes, >=54/60 unaided. Overlapping widths leave insertion cause unresolved; reports incompletely establish packing errors.
